purpose: A signal badge carried by nearly every creator in a domain has stopped describing the creator and started describing the field. Rule 17 states it once instead of repeating it on every card.
placementRule: Where the saturation is caused by the field, the note belongs on the category page — it tells a visitor something true about the domain they are entering. Where it is caused by our own inclusion rules, it is meta-commentary about how the list was built, and belongs on /how-this-list-was-built instead. Cause decides placement; the validator enforces the pairing.

entries.note: Nearly every fitness creator listed here sells coaching or a training program. That is how the credible end of this field is funded, so a paid program is the norm here rather than a mark against anyone. What still varies is whether the free videos stand on their own without the purchase, and the note on each card says which.

Most programming creators listed here sell a course or a paid track. That is close to universal among independent programming educators now, so read it as the default rather than as a warning. The question worth asking is whether the free videos are complete enough to learn from without buying anything, which the note on each card addresses.
entries.watch: Drifted from 83% to 71% between batches 16 and 22 as the domain filled out. One more creator without the badge drops it below the 70% threshold and this note should come down. Recorded because a note that survives only by a rounding margin is worth watching, not defending.

entries.note: Almost every productivity creator listed here sells a course, an app or a book built on the method they teach. This field is unusually self-referential that way: the product often is the method, so the incentive to present one system as more general than it really is comes built in. The note on each card names what the person sells and how hard they push it.

Most relationship creators listed here sell something built on the method — a course, a membership, a book, a retreat. In this field the people who have done the work to be worth listening to have generally turned it into a business, so a paid product is the norm rather than a signal about quality. Read the note on each card for what the specific product is and how hard the free videos push toward it.

Most marketing creators listed here sell a course, a tool or an agency's services. In a field with no licence and no gatekeeping, teaching in public is how practitioners are found and paid, so a product attached to the advice is the norm rather than a warning. What the badge still separates is who is selling the specific thing they are advising you to do.

whatTheBadgesTrack.title: What the badges actually track
paras: Some badges are on almost every card in a subject and almost none in another. The “practitioner” badge — meaning the person does this work outside of teaching it — is on every creator we list in marketing, business, fitness, programming and productivity, and on one in seven in philosophy.

That spread is the interesting part. It is not a rule we apply: 29 of the creators here carry no practitioner badge at all, and several of the best of them never practise what they explain. What it reflects is that skills you perform are usually taught by people who perform them, while subjects you reason about are more often taught by explainers, essayists and academics. Neither is better. They fail differently, which is worth knowing before you pick who to learn from.

The other two behave the same way. A professional qualification is common in relationships and health, where the subject sits near clinical practice, and absent in marketing and business, where no licence exists to hold. Citing sources is the norm in philosophy and rare in programming — not because programmers are careless, but because the claims are checked by running the code instead.

We got this wrong at first and said so on these pages for several weeks: we described these badges as our own inclusion rules showing up in the data. They are not. The correction, and the measurement that forced it, is on the record in the project's own files.

open.question: Is sells-course near-universal in business the way it is in fitness, productivity and programming?
open.answer: No. Measured at n=5 in batch 20: 3 of 5, 60% — below the 70% saturation threshold, so business gets no standing note for it and the per-creator badge still distinguishes creators within the domain.
open.caveat: n=5 is one creator above the measurement floor and 60% is one creator below the threshold, so this can flip. It is an answer, not a settled fact — re-check as business fills out.
open.history: Asked by the owner at 143 creators, when business had 2 and the question was unanswerable: 1 of 2 is 50% and means nothing. Left open rather than guessed at, and answered when the data existed.

retired.note: Almost every marketing creator listed here has a commercial interest in the field they are explaining. That is the shape of the supply rather than a run of bad apples: the independent practitioners in this field publish in newsletters and blogs, and most of the video that exists is hosted by companies selling the tools. The badge still separates what it should — who discloses the conflict, who is selling the specific thing they are advising you to do, and who is only hosting an outside practitioner's thinking on their own platform.
retired.history: Written EDITORIALLY at n=2 from the marketing domain pass, flagged for re-measurement. CONFIRMED at n=6 in batch 20: 5 of 6, 83%. FALSIFIED at n=9 in batch 23: 6 of 9, 67%, below the 70% threshold. Retired.
retired.why: The retirement is not a measurement wobble, it is the finding being tested. Rule 18 required a deliberate attempt to disprove the underlying claim that marketing's independent practitioners publish in text rather than video. That attempt found three of them working substantially in video — Alex Cattoni, Pat Flynn, 30 Minutes to President's Club — and none carries commercial-conflict. Looking for counterexamples produced counterexamples, which is what it is supposed to do.
retired.standing: The weak form of the marketing finding survives and is still on the record in UNVERIFIED.md: several named practitioners genuinely are not in video (Harry Dry 4 uploads, Seth Godin 7, copyhackers and backlinko unresolvable) and the SEO end of the domain remains vendor-hosted. The strong form — that the practitioners as a class are absent from video — is false.

sharedNotes.practitioner: Nearly every creator listed here does this work outside of teaching it, so the badge does not separate them from each other — read it as a description of the field rather than a distinction between these creators. Skills you perform tend to be taught by people who perform them; subjects you reason about are more often taught by explainers and academics. This is one of the former.
sharedNotes.credentialed: Most creators listed here hold a professional qualification. That is largely a fact about the field — this subject sits close enough to clinical practice that licensed people are the ones publishing — rather than something that sets these creators apart from each other. We did also weight qualifications more heavily here than elsewhere, which is our choice and is stated on the colophon.
sharedNotes.cites-research: Most creators listed here work from sources and say so, which in this subject is close to a definition of doing it properly rather than a mark of unusual rigour. The badge is the norm here; what still varies is how close to the primary texts they stay.

corrected.what: Fifteen entries were labelled cause: selection on the claim that these badges are near-universal because of our own inclusion rules — specifically that we 'do not list someone who explains a skill they have never practised'. The colophon said so to visitors.
corrected.whyItWasWrong: The claim was never tested and it is false. 29 of 196 creators — 15% — carry no practitioner badge at all, including Kane B, CrashCourse, Wireless Philosophy, Harvard Business Review and Heidi Priebe, so it plainly is not a requirement. Measured across domains, practitioner runs from 100% (marketing, business, fitness, programming, productivity) to 14% (philosophy). An inclusion rule would be near-uniform; a 100-to-14 spread is a fact about which subjects are taught by people who do them. credentialed and cites-research behave the same way — credentialed is 70% in relationships and 0% in marketing, cites-research is 71% in philosophy and 0% in programming. All three track the subject, not our preference.
corrected.correction: All fifteen entries reclassified to cause: field (relationships/credentialed to mixed, because a real editorial preference sits on top of the field structure there) and moved from the colophon to the category pages, which is where the placement rule sends a field-caused note. The colophon section that asserted the inclusion rule has been rewritten to report the actual finding.
corrected.foundBy: Rule 18, batch 26, during the sweep the owner asked for. The claim had been repeated in every batch report since batch 17 and never once checked.
